Each topic takes about 8 to 10 minutes. Mark a topic **shaky** and the app will bring it back in Recall and on your Ready page.
blocks.label: when

blocks.md: **An ADT says what a structure does, not how it's built**; a stack and a queue are two ADTs that differ only in which end things come out of.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: 'An abstract data type is a data type defined by its **behavior** (what it does), not its **implementation** (how it does it).' He wants this sentence, then an example.
Last in, first out. Add and remove at the **same end** (the top). push, pop, peek, isEmpty. Plates in a cafeteria. All O(1).
First in, first out. Add at the **back**, remove from the **front**. enqueue, dequeue, peek, isEmpty. A checkout line. All O(1) (with a circular array or a linked list with head and tail).
A chain of **nodes**; each holds a value and the **address of the next** node. You reach it through **head**; the last node's next is **null**. No index: getting the k-th item means walking k steps.

blocks.title: The same ADT, two builds
blocks.body: A stack can be built on an array (top = last filled index) or on a linked list (top = head). The ADT, push/pop/peek, is identical; only the inside differs. That's the whole point of an ADT.

Two linked-list bugs he calls out: (1) inserting after node B, write **X.next = B.next before B.next = X**, or the rest of the list is lost; (2) in a linked queue, when you dequeue the **last** item, set **tail = null** too.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** The full chapter draws every pointer change step by step.

sections.heading: 2. Loop invariants and insertion sort (Lectures 2 to 3)

blocks.md: **A loop invariant is a sentence that stays true every time the loop checks its condition**; proving it at the start, keeping it true each pass, and reading it at the end proves the loop correct.
blocks.label: think

rows: if true before an iteration, still true after it
when the loop stops, invariant + stop condition = the goal
blocks.title: The three parts

blocks.body: Keep a **sorted left part**. Take the next item (the **key**), slide it left past every bigger item, drop it in. Invariant: **a[0..j−1] is sorted** (the prefix handled so far).

rows: each key compares once and stays
blocks.title: Insertion sort's runtime

blocks.md: Insertion sort is **in place** (O(1) extra space) and **stable**: the test is strictly `a[i] > key`, so equal items never jump past each other.

blocks.body: Writing the invariant about the **whole** array ('the array is sorted') instead of the **prefix** ('a[0..j−1] is sorted'). An invariant must be true in the middle, when the job is half done.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** Lecture 3 from zero goes one idea at a time, with the code next to plain English and a video.

sections.heading: 3. Big-O, Omega, Theta and the growth ladder (Lecture 4)

blocks.md: **Big-O ignores constants and small terms and keeps only the shape of how the work grows** as the input gets big.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants **c > 0** and **n₀** with **f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀**. 'Past some size, f stays under a constant times g.'

rows: halving, with a full pass at each level (merge sort)
a loop inside a loop, both over the input
blocks.title: The growth ladder, slowest-growing first
Simplify
blocks.body:
T(n) = 3n² + 10n log n + 500

Keep the fastest-growing term, drop its constant: **Θ(n²)**.
Prove O(n²) with the definition: for n ≥ 1, 3n² + 10n log n + 500 ≤ 3n² + 10n² + 500n² = 513n², so c = 513, n₀ = 1.
Dropping a term that **isn't** a constant. n log n is not 'n times a constant': log n grows. O(n log n) stays O(n log n).

blocks.md: **Stuck?** Lecture 3 from zero explains what O, Ω and Θ are each for, with a video; Chapter 0 explains log from zero.

sections.heading: 4. Divide and conquer, binary search, merge sort (Lectures 4 to 5)

blocks.md: **Divide and conquer: split the problem into smaller copies of itself, solve those the same way, combine the answers.**
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Two sorted lists → one sorted list, by repeatedly taking the **smaller front item**. Θ(n) for n total items.

blocks.caption: Merge sort on [7, 3, 9, 1, 4, 8, 2, 6] as a 2.5-minute video: the splits going down, then every merge coming back up, with the call stack under the code. Use the chips to jump to a merge.

blocks.md: **Why n log n?** The halving makes **log n levels**; every level merges all n items once. n work × log n levels = **n log n**. That picture (the recursion tree) is the answer to 'explain merge sort's runtime'.

blocks.body: Saying merge sort sorts **in place**. It doesn't: merge writes into a temporary array, **O(n) extra space**. Insertion sort and heap sort are the in-place ones.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** Watch the video again at 0.75×, or step through merge in the chapter. log n vs n log n has its own slow section.

resources.label: log n vs n log n, slowly

blocks.md: **A recurrence writes a recursive algorithm's cost in terms of its own cost on smaller inputs**; the recursion tree adds that cost up row by row.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: An equation for T(n) using T of smaller inputs, plus a **base case**. Merge sort: **T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n**, T(1) = 1. Read it as: 'two calls on half the input, plus n work to merge'.
One box per call, with the work that call does **itself** inside. Total = sum of the **rows**. For aT(n/b) + f(n): row i has **aⁱ** calls of size **n/bⁱ**, and there are about **log_b n** rows.

blocks.title: Merge sort's tree
blocks.body:
Row 0: 1 call × n work = n
Row 1: 2 calls × n/2 = n
Row 2: 4 calls × n/4 = n
…
log₂ n rows, each costs n → total **n log n**
**Guess** the answer (usually from the tree), **assume** it holds for the smaller input, **substitute** into the recurrence, and **prove** it's ≤ c·(your guess). It's induction.
Forgetting the base case, or reading T(n−1) like T(n/2). T(n) = T(n−1) + 1 shrinks by **subtracting**: n levels, Θ(n). Halving gives log n levels.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** The chapter computes T(8) by hand before drawing the tree.

**For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a); whichever is bigger wins, and a tie costs an extra log n.** The cases are printed on the exam; the points are in doing the comparison cleanly.
blocks.label: think

rows: write **a** (number of calls), **b** (shrink factor), **f(n)** (work outside the calls)
compute **n^(log_b a)** ('b to what power gives a?'): the leaves' total work
is f(n) polynomially **smaller**, the **same**, or polynomially **bigger**?
smaller → **Θ(n^(log_b a))** · same → **Θ(n^(log_b a) log n)** · bigger (+ regularity) → **Θ(f(n))**
say '**does not apply**, because…' for the four bad shapes
blocks.title: The five moves

blocks.body: **a not constant** (n·T(n/2)); **subtracting instead of dividing** (T(n−1)); **only a log gap** (2T(n/2) + n/log n: not polynomially smaller); **case 3 without regularity** (n²(2 + cos n)). Write 'does not apply' plus the reason: that's the full-credit answer.
Calling n/log n 'smaller than n' and using case 1. The gap must be **polynomial** (exponents differ by some ε > 0). A log factor isn't. Does not apply.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** The chapter has a practice set with every case and every failure shape.
**A max-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is ≥ its children, so the biggest item is always at index 0.**
blocks.label: think

rows: let a[i] **sink**: swap with its **larger** child until it's bigger than both
buildHeap; then n times: swap root to the end, shrink, heapify(0)
O(n log n), O(1) space, **not stable**
append, then swap **up** while bigger than the parent
take a[0], move the last item to 0, heapify(0)

blocks.caption: The whole of heapsort in 2 minutes, on HW 8's array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]: build the heap, then peel off the max seven times. The tree and the array move together, so you see they are the same thing.

blocks.body: Mixing up index formulas: Poon is **0-based** (2i+1, 2i+2). The textbook (CLRS) is 1-based (2i, 2i+1). Use his.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** The chapter traces heapify and buildHeap line by line.
**Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller items are left of it and bigger ones right, then sorts each side the same way.** All the work is in partition; there's no combine step.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: pivot = **a[high]** (the last item). One left-to-right pass moves every item ≤ pivot into a left zone, then the pivot goes right after that zone, at **i + 1**, which is returned. The pivot is now in its **final sorted position**. Θ(n).

blocks.caption: Quicksort on the slide's array as a 2.5-minute video: code on the left, bars on the right. Every partition, every swap, and which calls are waiting on the stack. Use the chips to jump, or slow it to 0.75×.

blocks.title: The three n log n sorts (Poon's slide)

blocks.md: **Worst case:** every pivot is the largest or smallest item, so one side is empty and the other has n − 1: n + (n−1) + … = **n²**. With last-item pivots, that happens on **already sorted** input. Fixes: a **random** pivot, **median of three**.

blocks.body: Returning i instead of **i + 1** from partition, or counting the returned index from low instead of from 0 (it's an index into the **whole** array).

sections.heading: 9. The n log n limit and linear-time sorts (Lecture 10)

blocks.md: **Any sort that only compares pairs needs Ω(n log n) comparisons; counting, radix and bucket sort beat that by looking at the values themselves, but each only works on a certain kind of data.**
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Insertion, merge, heap and quicksort treat items like **closed boxes** they can only compare. Any such sort needs **Ω(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case. Poon states it; the proof is outside the course.

rows: integers in a small range [0, k]
count each value, cumulative counts = seats, place items **backwards**
stable-sort by the **last** digit, then the next, … d passes
n buckets, x goes to ⌊n·x⌋, sort each bucket, concatenate
blocks.title: Poon's summary table
Counting sort, the slide's example
blocks.body:
a = [4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], k = 4
count      = [2, 2, 1, 0, 1]   (two 0s, two 1s, …)
cumulative = [2, 4, 5, 5, 6]   (count[v] = how many items are ≤ v)
walk a backwards; seat = count[x] − 1; then count[x] −= 1
output     = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4]
Radix sort with an **unstable** inner sort gives **wrong** answers, not just slow ones: the earlier digits' order must survive. That's why counting sort walks **backwards** (it keeps it stable).

blocks.md: **Stuck?** The chapter traces all three on Poon's arrays.
**A hash table turns a key into an array index with a hash function, so insert, search and delete take O(1) on average**; collisions go into a chain at that slot.
blocks.label: think

blocks.caption: Poon's librarian analogy and the whole mechanism in 2.5 minutes. Use the chips to jump.

rows: key → slot number 0..m−1. Division: **k mod m**. Multiplication: **⌊m·(kA mod 1)⌋**
two different keys, same slot. Unavoidable when there are more possible keys than slots
each slot holds a linked list; insert at the **head** (O(1))
**n / m**, the average chain length. Search walks about α nodes
when α passes a limit (0.75), double m and re-insert everything: O(n) once in a while
the occasional O(n) resize spread over all the cheap inserts averages to O(1)
blocks.title: The whole lecture in six words
Chaining with h(k) = k mod 10
blocks.body:
insert 42, 17, 22, 37 (insert at head)
slot 2: 22 → 42
slot 7: 37 → 17
search(42): slot 2, walk 22, then 42: found in 2 steps

'Amortized O(1)' does **not** mean every call is O(1): one insert can cost O(n) when it triggers a resize. And it assumes a good hash function; one that sends everything to the same slot makes search **O(n)**.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** Start from the librarian story in the chapter; it maps every word.
**In a BST, every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is bigger, so search walks one path down: O(h).** Unlike a hash table, it keeps things in order.
blocks.label: think

blocks.caption: The lecture's mechanics as a 90-second animation: building Poon's example tree, insert 10, then the three delete cases on the original tree. Use the chips to jump, or slow it to 0.75×.

rows: one path down (min: keep going left)
search until you fall off; the new key becomes a **leaf**
leaf: remove · one child: child takes its place · two children: copy the **successor** (min of the right subtree) up, then delete it
right child? min of right subtree. Else: search from the root; the **last node where you stepped left**
blocks.title: Everything a BST does

blocks.md: **h is the catch.** Keys in mixed order: h ≈ log n, everything O(log n). Keys in **sorted** order: the tree is a chain, h = n − 1, everything **O(n)**. That's the problem AVL trees fix.

blocks.body: The BST rule is about whole **subtrees**, not just children. And in the two-children delete, forgetting step two: after copying the successor up, delete the old successor node.

blocks.md: **Stuck?** Poon's own successor videos, and the chapter's line-by-line traces.
**An AVL tree is a BST that keeps |H(left) − H(right)| ≤ 1 at every node by doing O(1) rotations after inserts and deletes, so its height, and every operation, stays O(log n).**
blocks.label: think

blocks.caption: AVL insert as a 95-second animation, with H and B under every node: Poon's Example 2 (the zig-zag LR case, two rotations), then all of HW 13 Problem 1. Use the chips to jump, or slow it to 0.75×.

blocks.body: **H(node)** = edges down to the deepest leaf (leaf 0, **null −1**). **B(node) = H(left) − H(right)**. Balanced if B is −1, 0 or 1; **B > 1** left-heavy, **B < −1** right-heavy.

columns: Path from the unbalanced node to the new key
blocks.title: Insert cases

rows: up to **O(log n)** (can cascade to the root)
**B(y)** of the heavier child (LL if ≥ 0, LR if < 0)
blocks.title: Insert vs delete
HW 13 Problem 1: insert 15, 20, 25, 10, 8
blocks.body:
15, 20: fine
25: 15 has B = −2, path right, right → RR: leftRotate(15), 20 on top
10: no rotation; 15 now leans left by 1
8: 15 has B = +2, path left, left → LL: rightRotate(15), 10 takes its place
Final: 20 (10 (8, 15), 25)
B is **left minus right** (left-heavy is positive), a missing child counts **−1**, and a zig-zag needs **two** rotations: one rotation just flips the problem to the other side.

blocks.title: Every sort

blocks.md: **Picking, in one breath:** need lookup by key only → hash table. Need order (min, ranges, sorted walk) → balanced BST (AVL). Need 'give me the most urgent next' → heap. Sorting small integers → counting/radix. General sorting with a guarantee → merge sort (stable) or heap sort (in place); fastest in practice → quicksort with a random pivot.
blocks.label: think

about the **prefix** handled so far, never the whole array
